attempts.raw_response: I took the little girl and brought her up as my own. She was a sweet child, quiet and thoughtful, with eyes that reminded me of her mother. When she was old enough, I sent her to school, and later she went to a business college. She got a position as a typist, and was doing well. Then she met this man, and he persuaded her to marry him. I was against it from the first. There was something about him I didn't like, though I couldn't say what it was. He had a way of looking at you that made you feel he was thinking something else entirely. But she wouldn't listen to me. She was young and in love, and she thought she knew better.

pair.human_continuation:
I train children for the stage, you know, me
and my sister, Ada Dyer; you've heard of her, I guess. The courts pay
us for her keep, but it isn't much, and I'm expecting to get what I
spent on her from what she makes on the stage. Two of them other
children are my pupils; but they can't touch Madie. She is a better
dancer an' singer than any of them. If it hadn't been for the Society
keeping her back, she would have been on the stage two years ago.
She's great, she is. She'll be just as good as her mother was."

Van Bibber gave a little start, and winced visibly, but turned it off
into a cough.
pair.prefix:
"I do," she said. "After the
divorce Ida came to me," she said, speaking more freely. "I used to be
in her company when she was doing 'Aladdin,' and then when I left the
stage and started to keep an actors' boarding-house, she came to me.
She lived on with us a year, until she died, and she made me the
guardian of the child.

source_document.title: Van Bibber and Others by Richard Harding Davis
